Updated request scope as of 5/17/24 refinement sent by Mr.Small:

We have put some thought into search restrictions and terms and here is what we would suggest:

(1) total time range of January 1, 2023 through July 31, 2023
(2) Anything that includes Juli Beth Hinds, Dr. Amy Lerner, urban studies and planning (USP), global policy & strategy (GPS), UCSD in conjunction with any of those terms
(3) Anything related to the regional water equity report or RDF
(4) Anything containing a reference to "Juli Beth Hinds, Dr Amy Lerner,  Geosyntec, USP, GPS, or the RWER or RDF", UCSD in conjunction with any of those terms sent to or from "Elise Ruiz, anyone at Murakawa Communications, anyone at Geosyntec including but not limited to Ken Susillo, Megan Otto, Stephanie Zinn; and anyone at the County including but not limited to Stephanie Gaines, Crystal Benham, Todd Snyder, Sarah Agassi, Eden Brukman, and Murtaza Baxamusa"

Original Request:

To Whom it may Concern:
I am writing on behalf of my client Juli Beth Hinds. On behalf of Ms. Hinds, please consider this a formal request pursuant to California Public Records Act, Government Code §6250 et seq. for copies of all DOCUMENTS of the County of San Diego Land Use & Environment Group that reference or relate to: Juli Beth Hinds; the Department of Urban Studies and Planning at the University of California San Diego; or Nathan Fletcher. ("DOCUMENTS" as used herein, shall be defined to mean any ''writing'' as that term is defined in Evidence Code section 250, including, but not limited to, correspondence, emails, texts, communications of any kind, recordings, tapes, computer print-outs, records, slides, photographs, notes, working papers, written analyses, memoranda, plans, telegraphs, telexes and transcriptions, electronic data, and notes or memoranda made by any telephone communications.) This request encompasses all DOCUMENTS dated or created between the dates of January 1, 2022 through the date of this letter.
I request delivery of these records to our firm's office, located at 402 W. Broadway, Suite 1270, San Diego, CA 92101, or we can arrange to pick them up at a reasonable location designated by the County.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Hi Joel,

Thanks again for your participation in the interview for this project.  We do have a couple follow up questions we’d like your input on below.  These are not meant to take more than 10-15 minutes of your time and it would greatly benefit our analysis.  Also, when able, we’d definitely be interested in viewing the maps you mentioned showing historic and current extents of agriculture, as well as ideal lands to increase agriculture throughout the region.

	a.	What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the San Diego and Imperial region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

Cost - heavy regional infrastructure investment creates a burden on consumers that they may not be able to support for uses that do not benefit them. Solutions need to be localized to individual communities to ensure resident buy-in and ability to pay. Communities need to be engaged to create community-specific drought resilience plans to prepare for reduced allocations at a neighborhood-level during drought conditions. To ease this burden, non-essential irrigation and consumptions should be eliminated and/or disincentivized with a heavily graduated pay scale based on per-capita volume for residential and commercial customers. This will incentivize further conservation, allowing for existing water supplies to be allocated more equitably. As an essential service for local residents, agricultural allocations should receive priority up to 1/3 of the regional allocation at special rates, so long as these farms contribute to the local food supply. We must prioritize use of precious water resources for urban greening in low-income neighborhoods and for agricultural production for local consumption in order to ensure regional resilience during drought conditions.

Just wanted you to see that Carl DeMaio is proposing a Contract to Reform California. Would love your feedback on the 10 points being proposed.

[https://storage.mlcdn.com/account_image/368629/msfpMWxCgs3mpXLi6LYLEmyLC3jTdKCJCHIUgU9Z.png]

For Immediate Release

November 25, 2024

Contact: Dylan Martin<mailto:dylan@capitolmedia.co>

760-710-7599

Assemblymember-elect Carl DeMaio Unveils 10-Point “Contract to Reform California”

“The 2024 election shows California voters are hungry for change, but to satisfy that demand, California Republicans must unite and commit to a comprehensive and common-sense reform package to fix the problems causing so many to flee our state.”

Taking a page from the successful “Contract with America” thirty years ago, incoming California State Assemblymember Carl DeMaio today unveiled a Contract to Reform California — a 10-point agenda that offers bold proposals to fix the state’s pressing problems. On December 2, 2024 — his first day in office — DeMaio plans to introduce 10 legislative proposals to advance the agenda.

“Exactly 30 years ago, the Contract with America catapulted Republicans from what was thought to be a permanent minority to a governing majority in the US Congress and ushered in an era of common-sense reform on national issues.

The 2024 election shows California voters are hungry for change, but to satisfy that demand, California Republicans must unite and commit to a comprehensive and common-sense reform package to fix the problems causing so many to flee our state.

The Contract to Reform California is a pledge to enact specific and detailed legislation to address the biggest problems facing our state — including reducing cost of living, reforming schools, balancing the budget, combatting crime, securing the border, reducing homelessness, restoring election integrity, and holding state politicians accountable.

If our Democratic colleagues won’t join us in advancing these reforms over the next two years, then we should be prepared to present our Contract to Reform California directly to the voters in the 2026 election.” – Carl DeMaio

DeMaio is available for further comment and interviews on the Contract to Reform California by phone, zoom or in-person.

ABOUT THE PROPOSAL:

[https://storage.mlcdn.com/account_image/368629/msfpMWxCgs3mpXLi6LYLEmyLC3jTdKCJCHIUgU9Z.png]

CONTRACT TO REFORM CALIFORNIA

1: Cost-of-Living Reduction Act

California’s cost-of-living crisis was caused by insane regulations and high taxes imposed by our price-gouging politicians. This law would provide each middle-class family with $2,500 in cost-of-living relief rebates annually — as well as suspend all state taxes and fees on gas and utilities until politicians reform state policies that spike costs. Once this model is proven successful in driving down energy and utility costs, it would be expanded to reduce costs in home insurance, housing, and healthcare. If we want politicians to address the cost crisis, we have to force them to pay the price — not our families!

2: Taxpayer Protection Act

This measure limits the ability of politicians to raise taxes — and prohibits them from imposing a new Mileage Tax, Exit Tax, or Wealth Tax — or increasing Gas or Car Taxes. The measure also restores a two-thirds vote requirement on local special tax increases and requires honest ballot titles with a “Tax Increase” warning be placed on any ballot measure that increases taxes.

3: Balanced Budget Accountability Act

We must balance the budget without tax hikes and cuts in important services. This measure would lead to a responsible consensus by requiring a two-thirds vote of both houses of the Legislature to pass the budget — or impose or increase taxes or fees. The measure would also reduce expense by cutting then capping total annual labor costs and imposing competitive sourcing reforms on all state agencies.

4: Education Choice and Parental Empowerment Act

The only way to truly empower parents is to give them financial freedom to choose the best school for their child. This law would provide $13,000 annually in education vouchers for every student — starting with middle-class and low-income families and then expanding the program.

5: Homelessness Reduction Act

This law would end the corrupt and wasteful “Housing First” homeless model currently used and replace it with a “People First” model, which will redirect funds to programs that require mental health and substance abuse treatment to address the root causes of homelessness. The law would also prioritize expansion of shelter beds over permanent supportive housing, impose work requirements on individuals receiving assistance, and require the removal of homeless camps near schools and in public areas. Developers that give campaign contributions would be barred from receiving funds.

6: End Reckless Release of Criminals Act

Passage of Prop 36 was just the first step in combatting the rising crime wave in California — we must also end “reckless release” of criminals across our state. This law would prohibit the early release of violent criminal and repeat offenders by repealing provisions of Prop 57 and prohibiting the placement of Sexually Violent Predators (SVPs) in residential communities. The law would also require mental health evaluations and referrals to proper treatment in any release decisions.

7: California Secure Borders Act
